props.title: The Last Remake of Beau Geste

sections.content: Marty Feldman's directorial debut **The Last Remake of Beau Geste (1977)** (1977) stands as a brilliant parody of the classic adventure film Beau Geste (1939), masterfully skewering both colonial-era military dramas and Hollywood's obsession with remakes. Feldman, fresh off his scene-stealing role in Young Frankenstein (1974), brings his distinctive brand of visual comedy and British wit to this often overlooked gem. The film follows the same basic premise as the original - twin brothers in the French Foreign Legion - but transforms it into a madcap comedy that shares DNA with other 1970s genre spoofs like **Blazing Saddles** (1974) and **Murder by Death** (1976).

sections.content: The film showcases an impressive ensemble cast including Michael York, Ann-Margret, and Peter Ustinov, who all embrace the absurdist tone while maintaining just enough gravitas to sell the parody. Feldman's direction borrows heavily from the Mel Brooks playbook he learned while making Silent Movie (1976), employing anachronistic jokes, fourth-wall breaks, and visual gags that would influence later military spoofs like **Stripes** (1981) and Hot Shots! (1991).

What sets **The Last Remake of Beau Geste** (1977) apart from other spoofs of its era is its meticulous attention to recreating the look and feel of 1930s adventure films while simultaneously undermining them. The cinematography by Alan Hume deliberately mimics the sweeping desert vistas of films like **The Four Feathers** (1939) and **Gunga Din** (1939), only to puncture their self-serious tone with perfectly timed physical comedy and surreal asides. sections.content: While not a massive box office success upon release, the film's influence can be seen in later genre parodies that combined high production values with lowbrow humor. Elements of Feldman's approach surface in films like **Airplane!** (1980) and **Top Secret!** (1984), where the comedy emerges from treating ridiculous situations with deadpan seriousness. The film also represents a crucial bridge between the more sophisticated parodies of the early 1970s and the broader spoofs that would dominate the 1980s.
